match.reason: The closest bank point, sci-protons-neutrons-electrons, covers the particles and charge balance but not the atomic number or mass number definitions the brief asks for, so adding those would be a new step rather than a small change.

draft.title: Protons, neutrons and electrons
card: A particle in the nucleus with a positive charge. The number of protons is the atomic number, and it decides which element an atom is.
A particle in the nucleus with no charge. It adds to the mass of the atom but not to its charge.
A tiny particle with a negative charge that moves around the nucleus. Its mass is very small compared with a proton or neutron.
The mass number is protons plus neutrons. A neutral atom has no overall charge, so it has as many electrons as protons. Neutrons = mass number - atomic number.
draft.remember: Atomic number = protons. Mass number = protons + neutrons. In a neutral atom, electrons = protons.

a.q: An atom of sodium has an atomic number of 11 and a mass number of 23. How many neutrons does it have?
a.why: Neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 23 - 11 = 12. The mass number is not the neutron count, because it also includes the 11 protons.
a.clue: Take the protons away from the mass number.

b.q: A neutral atom has 17 protons and 18 neutrons. Which row gives its atomic number, mass number and number of electrons?
b.why: The atomic number is the number of protons, 17. The mass number is 17 + 18 = 35. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so it has 17. The tempting option with 18 electrons confuses electrons with neutrons.
b.clue: A neutral atom has no overall charge, so its negative and positive particles match.
